doc.title: Clay Jenkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 18, 2016

title: Studio sessions in Los Angeles and playing with Joe LaBarbera and John Clayton
summary: He learned to ask what producers wanted on LA dates, while Joe LaBarbera and John Clayton let him play his own way.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Yeah. So different people have — you know I’ve had people come up and say, “you know I didn’t write a sharp nine on that chord.” I’m sorry. But some of it’s sort of serendipitous too, I must say. Sometimes I’ll try something just to see if it might stick. And it depends on the context. Like if I was called in out there in Los Angeles to record a solo over something else, a lot of times I’d just say, “what are you hearing?” Maybe, “why don’t you sing me something that you’re hearing.” Because I wanted to please. It wasn’t my time to be an artist. It was more my time to be a craftsman sometimes. So I learned that the hard way a few times. But if it’s like on my record, or if people call me to play on a record and the music’s very adventuresome then they usually let me play the way I play. Like I play a lot with this great drummer, actually originally from Rochester, Joe LaBarbera. Joe never tells me how to play. You know? Joe likes the way I play. And I love playing with him. Now on the Clayton-Hamilton band, I’ve been on that band for 30 years. And there was a time when I probably wasn’t fitting in as well, I think probably because I wasn’t as good a blues player as I needed to be. And that’s something I had to revisit, I still do. But now that I’m a better blues player I feel like they just know my voice is going to fit in certain situations, and in certain situations maybe not. But John is very respectful of me, the way I play.
